metadata.title: The AI spending spree is making the Fed's job harder

content.text:
Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh stepped into his new job with a case for lower interest rates on the back of an AI-fueled productivity boom. What he got instead was a $700 billion AI spending blitz that's demolishing his argument for rate cuts anytime soon with more price increases about to ripple through the U.S. economy.
With many tech companies like Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and more under the grip of AI-mania, they aren't flinching at taking on unprecedented spending commitments to expand their fleet of data centers and secure the equipment needed to run them. Now halfway through 2026, momentum at the Fed has shifted toward the possibility of interest rate hikes.
As the argument goes among AI's evangelists, employees adopting AI complete more tasks at a fraction of the time, and companies produce abundantly with the same number of workers. Profits and paychecks would then grow without stoking inflation. Warsh stuck to his bullish views on Wednesday, refusing to be labeled as an "AI doomer," and said the U.S. is only in "the first or second inning of this revolution."
Even at this early stage, policymakers believe the AI revolution is all but unstoppable. Generative AI is no longer viewed as a tool that accomplishes only low-stakes tasks. Most recognize it as an instrument capable of decimating millions of white-collar jobs through automation. Most Fed watchers and financial analysts, though, don't see evidence yet of broad labor productivity gains from AI that could justify a reduction in the Fed's borrowing rates. Fed policymakers last proceeded with a quarter-point cut at their December meeting and hit pause ever since.
Instead, they're zeroing in on the rapid data center buildout that's swallowing up an enormous amount of storage and memory chips — critical components in smartphones, video game consoles, cars, and more — as a culprit for another wave of inflation. The gobbling frenzy weakens the case for lower interest rates further, and policymakers tasked with assessing the fallout of AI are taking notice.
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said she had not observed enough "restraint" in the US economy, particularly among tech companies gobbling up critical semiconductor equipment at any price.
"What they say is that the demand is insatiable, that these companies — these hyper scalers — will pay almost any price for those inputs, and they need things built yesterday," Hammack, a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee, told CNBC on Wednesday. "I'm not hearing from these businesses that interest rates or credit spreads are a reason why they're holding back from investment and growth."
